title: Can a graph tell us who won a cricket match?
description: A double bar graph of runs per over for a blue team and a red team is read for who batted first, who won, two bar values and the target. Keeko thinks blue won because it has the tallest bar.
teaching_notes: One idea: a graph can answer questions it never asks aloud, if we read the scale, the markers and where the bars stop. Watch for students who pick the winner from the tallest bar.

source: Cricket match graph: runs per over for the blue team and the red team; who batted first, who won, blue's over 12, red's lowest over, and whether the target is easy to find
video_script.why: The child can read a bar and its scale, and now reads a match story from two sets of bars.
video_script.substitution: The book's own runs per over graph, with a blue team and a red team.
video_script.anchor: Double bar graph of runs per over, overs 1 to 20, scale 1 unit = 5 runs. Blue bars run through all 20 overs with several wicket circles. Red bars stop after over 18 with no wicket circles.
video_script.wrong_answer: blue won because it has the tallest bar
video_script.wrong_move: Picks the winner from the single tallest bar instead of reading where each team's bars stop.
video_script.payoff_line: Blue batted first and red won.

final_answer.value: Blue batted first and red won; blue scored about 15 in over 12; red's lowest was over 4 with about 2 runs; the target needs 20 bars added, so it is not quick
final_answer.spoken: blue batted first and red won; blue about fifteen runs in over twelve; red's lowest was over four, about two runs; the target is not quick to find

maths_rules: scale: 1 unit = 5 runs; red's bars stop after over 18 with no wicket circles, so red reached the target early
blue's over 12 bar reaches the 15 guideline: 3 units x 5 = 15 runs (accept 14 to 16)
red's shortest bar is over 4: about 2 runs (accept 1 to 3)
target = blue's total + 1, which needs all 20 of blue's bars added
video_script.design: One idea: read the story of a match from where the bars stop. The two sets of bars sit in the anchor; on the board the scale reads two bars and the stopping point of red's bars gives the winner.
open_questions: The bar values (blue about 15 in over 12, red lowest in over 4 at about 2) and the facts that red stops after over 18 with no wickets come from the worklist; the extracted book text has no bar values for this graph. Check against the printed graph.
